extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in public relations, propaganda, political communication, and history of mass persuasion
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of principles and thematic criteria from Edward Bernays' Propaganda (1928) as presented in the Internet Archive item — focused on techniques for shaping public opinion and the domains to which propaganda applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: The scientific technique of shaping and manipulating public opinion ("engineering of consent")
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernays 'pioneered the scientific technique of shaping and manipulating public opinion, which he famously dubbed "engineering of consent."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat persuasion as an engineered, systematic practice: use research, testing, and targeted messaging to shape collective attitudes rather than relying on ad-hoc appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wartime propaganda methods to package and sell ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: During World War I Bernays was part of the CPI, 'a powerful propaganda apparatus that was mobilized to package, advertise and sell the war to the American people...'; the CPI became a blueprint for later marketing strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame communications as a packaged product that can be advertised and sold; borrow structuring and distribution techniques from large-scale campaigns (e.g., wartime information programs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of psychological theory into public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernays incorporated ideas of Walter Lippmann and Sigmund Freud and advocated applying psychological insight to manipulation of the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground messaging in an understanding of unconscious motives, social psychology, and media framing to increase persuasive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda as a tool for democratic and corporate manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernays became an outspoken proponent of propaganda as a tool for democratic and corporate manipulation of the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize propaganda's dual use: for shaping democratic opinion and for corporate ends; craft communications with awareness of ethical and institutional implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying propaganda across societal domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda is applicable to 'government, politics, art, science and education' and other areas according to Bernays' vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt persuasive strategies to the norms and channels of each domain (e.g., political messaging vs. educational campaigns vs. cultural influence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing Chaos
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title listed in the item: 'Organizing Chaos.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implying a criterion: communications should create coherent narratives out of complex or disordered information to guide public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: The New Propaganda
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on modernized, systematic methods of persuasion distinct from earlier ad-hoc or traditional rhetoric; messages should leverage mass media and modern organizational techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: The New Propagandists
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the role and responsibilities of modern communicators/PR practitioners: specialize in creating and directing campaigns rather than simple message delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Psychology of Public Relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title listed: 'The Psychology of Public Relations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate communications for psychological targeting: appeals to emotion, use of symbols, authority cues, and mechanisms to influence group behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business and the Public
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title listed: 'Business and the Public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how corporate messaging aligns business interests with public sentiment; craft narratives that legitimize commercial objectives to broad audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda and Political Leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title listed: 'Propaganda and Political Leadership.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how leaders use messaging to consolidate support and shape political reality; communications should be tailored to leadership roles and institutional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's Activities and Propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title listed: 'Women's Activities and Propaganda.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize target-group-specific campaigns: design messaging that engages particular demographics (here, women) through culturally resonant channels and activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda for Education
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use educational institutions and pedagogical framing to inculcate desired ideas; long-term persuasion can be achieved through curricula and instruction design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda in Social Service
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title listed: 'Propaganda in Social Service.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage social services and charitable framing as vehicles for persuasion: align public-good narratives with organizational goals to gain trust and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and Science
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate aesthetic and scientific approaches: craft messages that are both emotionally resonant (art) and systematically designed (science).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Mechanics of Propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter title listed: 'The Mechanics of Propaganda.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the concrete tools and channels (media, events, spokespeople, symbols) used to implement campaigns; effectiveness depends on precise tactical execution.
